posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
I wouldn't be so quick to buy a 215. I don't think it's quite the same thing as a 315. My memory is very foggy on this, however, so I say this without any proof, either through personal experience or what I've heard. Maybe it was something I read on Sam's Laser FAQ, but I can't remember. But the main thing is that I've never heard a report of someone using one for holography. That might say something. (We all should know about the huge quantity of 532nm lasers that are unsuitable for holography.) On the other hand, maybe they work as well as a 315, without any reports reaching my attention. It's a risk to buy one, I would say.

If you want a low-power 532 laser that's got a proven track record for holography, I would use one of the "microgreen" lasers as have been talked about on this forum. Better yet, save up for a 315 (watch eBay and other online sellers). The extra power might come in handy at a later date. Alternately, look for one of the 532 series, though it might cost a bit more than a 315.

On the other hand, those 215's were so cheap that it wouldn't have been a catastrophe if you bought one and it didn't work.

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
215M or not 215M, that is the question. Perusing Sam’s Laser FAQ’s rather cursorily, the only major difference that I could find between the 215 and the 315 is that the 215 is missing the TEC for the resonator, which could mean trouble. But he says the optical design is the same. Since there is no TEC, stability may be an issue, but then again, once everything is temp stabilized it could be copasetic, for how often do we run gas lasers at room temperature and after a while they seem to find a happy mode.

I do have at my disposal a Spectra-Physics scanning Fabry-Perot Spectrum Analyzer, so if anyone has one of these 215’s or any other laser whose linewidth they would like to see, it can be checked.

Too bad about those lasers disappearing; I guess my “blessing” turned into a curse. I didn’t go for them, as I have a 315, but I think we might be able to see where they went. They may pop up here, or at Photon Lexicon. That site seems to have 10X the appeal, as when I go there it’s not only myself but maybe a dozen others viewing, as compared to here where it’s usually just lonely old me and the Googlebot.

But 10 to 20 mW of green at that price is amazing! I thought my M-G 7 mW He-Ne was a bargain at less than $100/mW back in ’81!

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
The 215M is nearly the same as the 315M, but there is less temperature control. The 315M has very accurate temperature control to keep cavity length constant and a separate temperature control for the KTP crystal.

The temperature control on the KTP is very important in the 315M because it is that part, combined with a Brewster window that guarantees single mode behaviour.

I once phoned with a technical representative of Coherent because I could get one cheaply. He said that the 215M lacks this accurate temperature control and is therefore absolutely not guaranteed to be single mode. Now I am not sure which TEC is missing in the 215M. I don't know if it is the TEC that stabilizes the cavity length or the one that stabilizes the KTP temperature. But I decided it was not worth the risk to buy one.

posts.author: Konrad
posts.content_md:
Ok, my quick and dirty review. I got power supply and assembled everything on large heatsink

![Image](http://img15.imageshack.us/img15/1733/c215m.jpg)

Laser works excellent, first I though that laser is dead because beam start shining after 70 seconds. Later I setup interferometer and I got rock solid fringes without mode hops (I observed for few minutes). Next I setup single beam transmission arrangement - I put ruler with 62cm depth and after exposing and developing I got excellent hologram, all ruler is visible from start to end. Conclusion - it looks Compass 215M-10 is another great laser for holography, I'm going to keep it.
